question: What is a Git branch?
options: A lightweight movable pointer to a commit
A full copy of the working directory stored in a separate folder
A server-side repository that hosts shared code
A fixed label that can never move once created
explanation: A branch is just a named reference to a commit. When you commit on the branch, the pointer moves forward automatically. This is why creating branches in Git is cheap and fast, unlike copying a directory tree.

question: Assume Git 2.23 or later. Which command creates a new branch named feature/login and switches to it in one step?
options: git branch feature/login
git checkout feature/login
git switch -c feature/login
git switch feature/login
explanation: git switch with -c creates the branch and switches to it. Plain git branch only creates the branch without switching. git switch and git checkout without a creation flag only work for a branch that already exists.

question: What does HEAD normally refer to in a Git repository?
options: The very first commit of the repository
The currently checked-out commit, usually through the current branch reference
The default branch on the remote server
The oldest entry in the reflog
explanation: HEAD marks where you are now. Normally it points to a branch, and that branch points to its latest commit. Committing moves the branch, and HEAD follows it.

question: What does a pull request (or merge request) represent?
options: A core Git command that downloads and merges remote changes
A special Git object type stored in the .git directory
A tag that marks a release candidate
A feature of a hosting platform that proposes merging one branch into another and enables review and discussion
explanation: Pull requests are not part of core Git. They are provided by platforms such as GitHub, GitLab, and Bitbucket. The Git command that downloads and merges remote changes is git pull, which is a different thing.

question: What is the difference between git fetch and git pull?
options: git fetch merges remote changes, while git pull only downloads them
They are identical commands with different names
git pull only works on the main branch
git fetch only updates remote-tracking branches, while git pull fetches and then integrates the changes into the current branch
explanation: git fetch downloads new commits and updates references like origin/main without touching your working branch. git pull is fetch followed by a merge (or a rebase if configured). The trap is thinking fetch changes your local branch.

question: When can Git perform a fast-forward merge?
options: Only when there are merge conflicts to resolve
When the current branch tip is an ancestor of the branch being merged, so the pointer can simply move forward
Only when both branches contain exactly the same number of commits
Only when the merge is run with the --squash option
explanation: If the target branch has no commits of its own since the branches diverged, Git just moves the target pointer to the other branch tip. No new merge commit is needed.

question: Assume main is an ancestor of feature/search. What does the --no-ff option do in this merge?
code:
git switch main
git merge --no-ff feature/search
options: Performs a fast-forward and moves only the main pointer
Aborts the merge with an error
Creates a merge commit even though a fast-forward was possible
Rebases feature/search onto main before merging
explanation: --no-ff forces a merge commit even when a fast-forward is possible. This keeps the fact that a feature branch existed visible in the history.

question: What is the result of a squash merge of a feature branch into main?
options: The changes are added as one new commit on main, and the individual feature commits do not become part of main's history
Every feature commit is copied to main with its original hash
A merge commit with two parents is always created
The feature branch is deleted and its commits are permanently erased from the repository
explanation: A squash merge combines all changes into a single new commit on the target branch. The original commits are not ancestors of that commit, which keeps history short but loses the individual commits on main.

question: What does git rebase do to the commits of the current branch?
options: It merges them into a single commit automatically
It replays them on top of a new base, creating new commits with new hashes
It deletes them and keeps only the target branch history
It copies them to the remote without changing local history
explanation: Rebase takes your commits and re-applies them on a different base commit. Because the parent changes, each replayed commit gets a new hash even if its content is similar.

question: Which rule should a developer remember about rebasing?
options: Always rebase main onto feature branches
Rebase only works for branches that have never been committed to
Rebase should be used instead of every merge
Do not rebase commits that have already been pushed and are used by other people
explanation: Rebasing rewrites history. If others have based work on the original commits, their history and yours diverge and cause confusing conflicts. Rebase local, unshared commits freely.

question: When does a merge conflict occur?
options: When two branches changed the same part of a file in different ways and Git cannot decide automatically
Whenever two branches contain different commit counts
Whenever a branch name contains a slash
Whenever a pull request has more than one reviewer
explanation: Git merges non-overlapping changes automatically. A conflict appears only when overlapping changes (or a change versus a deletion) cannot be combined without a human decision.

question: A developer commits this file by accident after a conflicted merge, leaving the conflict markers in. What happens when the file is compiled?
options: It prints Hello
It prints Hi
A compile-time error occurs because the conflict markers are not valid Java
It prints both Hello and Hi
explanation: Git inserts the marker lines into the file text. They are not Java syntax, so the compiler rejects the file. This is why conflicts must be resolved and the markers removed before committing.

question: A merge stopped with a conflict in App.java and the developer has edited the file to the correct content. What is the right next step?
options: git merge --abort
git add App.java, then git commit (or git merge --continue)
git stash, then git pull
git rm App.java
explanation: Staging the resolved file tells Git the conflict is resolved. Then committing (or git merge --continue) finishes the merge. Abort would throw the work away.

question: Which command abandons an in-progress conflicted merge and returns to the state before the merge started?
options: git reset --soft HEAD~1
git commit --amend
git revert HEAD
git merge --abort
explanation: git merge --abort restores the pre-merge state of the branch and working tree. The other commands operate on existing commits and do not cancel a merge in progress.

question: What is the remote-tracking branch origin/main?
options: A branch on the server that you edit directly
A copy of main stored in the .gitignore file
A local read-only reference recording the last-known state of main on origin, updated by fetch
A tag that always points to the first commit of main
explanation: Remote-tracking branches are local bookmarks of remote state. You cannot commit to them directly, and they move only when you fetch, pull, or push.

question: What does the -u option do in this command?
code: git push -u origin feature/cart
options: It sets the upstream so later git push and git pull on this branch know the remote branch
It uploads untracked files only
It forces the push even when history has diverged
It uses a unique temporary branch name on the remote
explanation: -u is short for --set-upstream. It links the local branch to origin/feature/cart, so later commands work without extra arguments and status can show ahead/behind counts.

question: After rewriting a feature branch, why is git push --force-with-lease preferred over git push --force?
options: It refuses to overwrite the remote branch if it changed since you last fetched it
It makes the push run faster
It automatically rebases the branch before pushing
It skips all repository hooks
explanation: --force-with-lease checks that the remote branch is still where you expect. If a teammate pushed meanwhile, the push is rejected instead of silently destroying their commits.

question: Which statement best summarizes branch protection rules on a hosting platform?
options: They encrypt the contents of a branch
They prevent a branch from being deleted from a developer's local clone
They restrict direct pushes and can require reviews and passing status checks before changes are merged into important branches
They automatically resolve all merge conflicts
explanation: Branch protection enforces team policy on branches like main. Typical rules are required reviews, required checks, and blocking force pushes.

question: Convention: every merge of two diverged branches creates exactly one merge commit. How many commits are reachable from main at the end?
code:
main = commits [A, B]
feature = branch created from main at B
feature adds commit C
main adds commit D
merge feature into main (no conflicts)
print number of commits reachable from main
explanation: Main contains A, B, and D. The merge brings in C and adds one merge commit M. That makes A, B, C, D, and M, which is five commits.

question: After the rebase described below, which statement is true?
code:
main:    A - B - D
feature: A - B - C
rebase feature onto main (no conflicts)
options: feature becomes A - B - C - D and C keeps its original hash
feature becomes A - B - D - C' where C' is a new commit with a different hash than C
feature gets a merge commit joining C and D
main becomes A - B - D - C
explanation: Rebase replays C on top of D. Since the parent of the replayed commit changed, it is a new commit (C'). Main is not modified by this rebase.

question: A developer wants to start a new branch hotfix/payment from the latest origin/main without checking out main first. Which command does this?
options: git branch hotfix/payment
git switch hotfix/payment
git switch -c hotfix/payment origin/main
git merge origin/main hotfix/payment
explanation: The start point argument after the branch name sets where the new branch begins. Without it, the new branch starts from the current HEAD instead.

question: Complete the command so that it deletes the local branch only if it is fully merged and refuses otherwise.
code: git branch ____ feature/login
options: -d
-D
-m
-r
explanation: -d is the safe delete and fails when the branch has unmerged commits. -D forces deletion, -m renames, and -r works on remote-tracking branches.

question: Which command deletes the branch feature/login on the remote named origin?
options: git branch -dr origin/feature/login
git push origin --delete feature/login
git remote remove feature/login
git fetch origin feature/login
explanation: git push origin --delete removes the branch on the server. The git branch -dr form only deletes the local remote-tracking reference and leaves the server branch untouched.

question: What does git cherry-pick followed by a commit hash do?
options: Deletes that commit from the history
Merges the entire branch that contains the commit
Tags the commit as a release
Applies the changes introduced by that commit as a new commit on the current branch
explanation: Cherry-pick copies the effect of one commit onto the current branch as a new commit with a new hash. It is useful for porting a hotfix to a release branch.

question: A bad commit is already pushed to the shared main branch. Which approach safely undoes it without rewriting shared history?
options: git reset --hard HEAD~1 followed by git push --force
git rebase -i to drop the commit followed by a force push
git revert with the commit hash, which creates a new commit that reverses it
git commit --amend followed by a force push
explanation: git revert adds a new commit that undoes the changes, so history stays intact for everyone. The other approaches rewrite shared history and require force pushes.

question: What does git reset --hard HEAD~1 do?
options: Moves the current branch pointer back one commit and discards the staged and working tree changes to match it
Creates a new commit that reverses the last commit
Deletes the remote copy of the last commit
Switches to the previous branch
explanation: --hard resets the branch pointer, the index, and the working tree. Uncommitted changes are lost, which is the main danger of this command.

question: What is the purpose of git stash?
options: To permanently delete uncommitted changes
To push changes to a hidden remote
To compress old commits to save disk space
To temporarily shelve uncommitted changes so the working tree is clean
explanation: git stash saves modified tracked files on a stack and restores a clean working tree. Later git stash pop re-applies them.

question: Which description fits trunk-based development?
options: Developers keep long-lived feature branches for months
Developers use short-lived branches merged to main frequently, hiding unfinished work behind feature flags
Each developer works only in a personal fork and never merges
Releases are built only from a develop branch
explanation: Trunk-based development keeps branches short so integration happens often. Unfinished features are merged but disabled by flags, which reduces large painful merges.

question: Which statement correctly compares Git Flow and trunk-based development?
options: Git Flow has no release branches
Git Flow uses long-lived develop and release branches, while trunk-based development keeps branches short-lived
Trunk-based development requires a separate branch for every release
Both strategies forbid feature branches
explanation: Git Flow has structured long-lived branches such as develop and release/*. Trunk-based development prefers a single main line with small, frequent merges. The trade-off is process structure versus integration speed.

question: An unfinished feature is merged to main with its flag disabled. What is the output? Assume Java 17.
options: new:100
A compile-time error
legacy:100
explanation: The flag is false, so the legacy branch runs and prints legacy:100. Merged code can ship safely while a feature flag keeps it inactive.

question: In a three-way merge, what is the merge base?
options: The common ancestor commit of the two branches being merged
The newest commit on the remote
The first commit ever made in the repository
The commit that has the most parents
explanation: Git compares each branch tip with their common ancestor to see what each side changed. Both change sets are then combined.

question: What does this command list?
code: git log main..feature/search
options: Commits reachable from main but not from feature/search
Commits that exist in both branches
Commits reachable from feature/search but not from main
Only the files that differ between the branches
explanation: The A..B syntax means commits reachable from B but not from A. It is a quick way to see what a pull request would add to main.

question: What does git diff main...feature (three dots) show?
options: All differences between the two branch tips
Only the commits unique to main
The list of merge conflicts
The changes made on feature since it diverged from main, compared against their merge base
explanation: Three dots compare the merge base with the feature tip. This matches what a pull request typically displays, without including later changes made only on main.

question: Which practice makes a pull request easiest to review?
options: Combine many unrelated changes in one large PR
Keep it small and focused, with a clear description and passing checks
Skip the description to save time
Push directly to main after approving your own change
explanation: Small, focused PRs are reviewed faster and more accurately. A clear description and green checks reduce back-and-forth.

question: Which statement about the Rebase and merge option on a pull request is correct?
options: It always creates a merge commit
It squashes every commit into one
It replays each feature commit onto the target branch without creating a merge commit
It deletes the target branch afterwards
explanation: Rebase and merge keeps the individual commits, but as new commits on top of the target, resulting in linear history. Squash merge, in contrast, collapses them into one.

question: What happens to the commits when you delete a branch with git branch -D?
options: Only the branch pointer is removed. The commits stay in the repository until they become unreachable and are garbage-collected
All commits on that branch are erased immediately
The commits are moved to main automatically
The remote branch is deleted as well
explanation: A branch is just a pointer. Deleting it does not remove commits. They can often be recovered through the reflog until garbage collection removes them.

question: What does detached HEAD mean?
options: The repository has no commits
The remote branch has been deleted
HEAD file is missing from the .git directory
HEAD points directly to a commit instead of a branch, so new commits are not on any branch
explanation: This happens when you check out a commit hash or tag. Commits made there can be lost when you switch away unless you create a branch to keep them.

question: A developer made commits in detached HEAD state and wants to keep them. Which command does this?
options: git switch main
git switch -c rescue-work
git reset --hard main
git branch -d rescue-work
explanation: Creating a branch at the current commit gives the new commits a name, so they stay reachable. Switching away without it risks losing them.

question: What does git pull --rebase do?
options: Replays your local unpushed commits on top of the fetched upstream commits, avoiding an extra merge commit
Deletes your local commits and keeps the remote ones
Squashes all local commits into one
Pushes your commits to the remote before fetching
explanation: It fetches and then rebases local commits onto the upstream branch, so the history stays linear instead of getting a merge commit.

question: What is the purpose of a CODEOWNERS file in a repository hosted on a platform that supports it?
options: It stores the license text of the project
It lists the people who may delete the repository
It defines owners for paths so they are automatically requested to review changes touching those paths
It lists the files Git should ignore
explanation: CODEOWNERS maps file patterns to people or teams. When a pull request changes matching files, those owners are requested for review, and protection rules can require their approval.

question: After a feature PR was squash-merged, git branch -d feature/login on the developer's local clone fails with a not fully merged error. Why?
options: The branch name contains a slash
Git does not allow deleting branches once they have been pushed
The squash commit on main is a new commit, so the original feature commits are not ancestors of main
The remote branch must be deleted first
explanation: git branch -d checks whether the branch commits are reachable from the current branch. A squash merge creates a different commit, so the check fails even though the content was merged. The branch can be deleted with -D once you are sure.

question: What does a required status check on a protected branch mean?
options: The pull request cannot be merged until the configured checks, such as CI jobs, have passed
The pull request is merged automatically after one hour
Only the repository owner may see the check results
Checks run only after the merge is completed
explanation: Required status checks block merging until the named checks report success. This keeps broken code from reaching the protected branch.

question: What is the purpose of this command?
code: git rebase -i HEAD~3
options: Rebases the branch onto the remote main
Lets the developer interactively edit, reorder, or squash the last three commits
Creates three new empty commits
Reverts the last three commits and pushes them
explanation: The -i flag opens an interactive todo list for the last three commits, where you can pick, reword, squash, or drop them. It rewrites history, so use it on unshared commits.

question: Which command lists local branches whose tips are already reachable from the current branch?
options: git branch --no-merged
git branch -r
git branch -vv
git branch --merged
explanation: --merged lists branches already merged into the current one, which are good candidates for cleanup. --no-merged shows the opposite.

question: Which command shows each local branch together with its upstream branch and ahead/behind counts?
options: git branch -vv
git branch -a
git branch --list
git remote -v
explanation: -vv is verbose twice and adds the tracked upstream and how many commits the branch is ahead or behind. git remote -v shows remote URLs, not branch tracking.

question: Complete the command so that it removes stale remote-tracking branches for branches already deleted on origin.
code: git remote ____ origin
options: add
show
prune
rename
explanation: git remote prune origin deletes local remote-tracking references whose remote branch no longer exists. git remote show only displays information and the other subcommands need extra arguments or do something different.

question: In Git Flow, which workflow best handles an urgent production fix?
options: Commit the fix directly on a feature branch
Wait for the next release branch and include it there
Branch from develop, fix, and merge only into develop
Branch a hotfix from main, fix, then merge it back into main and into develop
explanation: The hotfix branch starts from production code on main. Merging it back to both main and develop ensures the fix is not lost in the next release.

question: Git refuses this command and says local changes would be overwritten by checkout. What is the best fix?
code: git switch release/2.0
options: Run git merge --abort
Commit or stash the local changes, then switch again
Delete the .git directory and clone again
Run git push --force
explanation: The uncommitted changes touch files that differ in the target branch, so switching would lose them. Committing or stashing first keeps the work safe.

question: A rebase stopped on a conflict and the developer wants to cancel it completely. Which command does this?
options: git rebase --abort
git merge --abort
git reset --soft HEAD
git commit --amend
explanation: git rebase --abort returns the branch to the state before the rebase started. git merge --abort is only for merges in progress.

question: During git rebase main on a feature branch, which meaning do the labels ours and theirs have in conflict resolution?
options: ours is the feature commit being replayed, and theirs is main
ours and theirs always mean the same thing as in a merge
ours is the branch being rebased onto (main side), and theirs is the feature commit being replayed
ours refers to the remote, and theirs to the local branch
explanation: Rebase works by checking out the new base and replaying your commits onto it, so the roles look swapped compared with a merge. This is a classic source of mistakes when resolving rebase conflicts.

question: Two branches merge without any textual conflict. One renamed Util.calc to Util.compute, and the other added a call to Util.calc in Main. What happens when the merged code is compiled?
options: It prints 10
A compile-time error occurs because the method calc cannot be found
It compiles and throws NoSuchMethodError at runtime
It prints 5
explanation: Git merged different files cleanly, but the result is semantically broken. Because the call is resolved at compile time, javac reports cannot find symbol. A clean merge does not guarantee a working build, which is why CI runs on pull requests.

question: In Git Flow, what is the purpose of a release branch?
options: To store experimental work that may never ship
To replace the main branch permanently
To hold the developer's personal drafts
To stabilize a version for release, allowing only bug fixes and release preparation
explanation: A release branch freezes features for the upcoming version. Only fixes and release tasks are added, while new feature work continues on develop.

question: How does a Git tag differ from a branch?
options: A tag moves forward automatically with each new commit
A tag can only be created on the remote
A tag is stored only in the working tree
A tag normally stays fixed on one commit, while a branch moves as new commits are added
explanation: Tags mark a specific commit, often a release version. Branches are expected to advance as work continues.

question: What is printed by this pseudocode?
code:
main points to commit 3
feature = new branch at commit 3
feature adds commits 4 and 5
switch to main
merge feature into main
merge commits = 0
if merge was fast-forward then keep merge commits = 0 else add 1
print main tip number, merge commits
explanation: Main had no new commits, so the merge is a fast-forward. The main pointer moves to commit 5 and no merge commit is created, so the output is 5 0.

question: Which pull request merge strategy keeps a linear history while preserving each individual feature commit?
options: Squash and merge
Create a merge commit with --no-ff
Rebase and merge
Close the pull request without merging
explanation: Rebase and merge replays each commit on top of the target, so history stays linear and the individual commits remain. Squash also gives linear history but collapses them into one.

question: What is the git reflog useful for?
options: Recovering commits after a mistaken reset or branch deletion by showing where HEAD and branch tips pointed previously in the local repository
Listing the commits stored on the remote server
Viewing the list of pull requests
Showing who owns each file
explanation: The reflog is a local history of reference movements. Even if a branch was deleted or reset, you can often find the old commit there and recreate a branch from it.

question: After rebasing a feature branch that was already pushed, a plain git push is rejected. Why?
options: The remote does not accept rebased branches in any form
The rewritten history is no longer a fast-forward of the remote branch, because the old commits are not ancestors of the new ones
The branch name must be changed after a rebase
Git requires a pull request to exist first
explanation: Rebase created new commits with new hashes. The remote branch still has the old ones, so the push would not be a simple fast-forward and is rejected unless forced, ideally with --force-with-lease.

question: What does git merge --squash feature/x do on its own?
options: Creates a merge commit with two parents
Fast-forwards main to the feature tip
Deletes the feature branch
Stages the combined changes but does not create the commit, and no merge relationship is recorded
explanation: After --squash the changes are in the index, and you must run git commit yourself. The resulting commit has only one parent, so Git does not know the feature branch was merged.

question: A protected branch requires branches to be up to date before merging, and a pull request shows it is out of date with the base branch. Which action satisfies this?
options: Update the feature branch by merging or rebasing the base branch into it and pushing
Delete the base branch
Close and reopen the pull request
Rename the feature branch
explanation: The rule needs the feature branch to contain the latest base commits. Merging or rebasing the base into the feature branch, then pushing, achieves that and re-triggers checks.

question: A developer is on branch feature/login and runs the command below. What happens?
code: git pull origin main
options: It switches the developer to main
It overwrites feature/login with origin/main
It fetches origin/main and merges it into the currently checked-out feature/login
It deletes main on the remote
explanation: git pull integrates into the current branch, not into main. The result is that feature/login receives the latest main changes, and a merge commit or conflicts may appear.

question: What is the main goal of continuous integration (CI)?
options: To deploy every change to production by hand each night
To replace code reviews with automated tools
To merge changes frequently and automatically build and test them so integration problems are found early
To store compiled files in a permanent archive
explanation: CI means developers integrate small changes often, and an automated build and test run verifies each integration. The value is early detection of problems, not replacing reviews or deployment.

question: Which statement correctly distinguishes continuous delivery from continuous deployment?
options: Continuous delivery keeps every change releasable but a person approves the production release, while continuous deployment releases automatically after the pipeline passes
Continuous delivery never uses automated tests, while continuous deployment always does
Continuous delivery means deploying only once a year, while continuous deployment means once a month
They are exactly the same practice with two names
explanation: Both practices keep the code in a deployable state. The difference is the last step: delivery stops at a manual approval, deployment pushes to production automatically.

question: What is a stage in a CI pipeline?
options: A physical server that stores the code
A Git branch used only for releases
A library that the project depends on
A logical phase of the pipeline, such as build, test, or deploy, that groups one or more jobs
explanation: Stages organize the pipeline into ordered phases. Jobs inside a stage can usually run in parallel, and the next stage starts after the previous one succeeds.

question: What does the term pipeline as code mean?
options: The pipeline can only be created by writing Java code
The pipeline definition lives in a versioned file in the repository, such as a Jenkinsfile or a YAML file
The pipeline runs only on the developer's laptop
The pipeline code is compiled into the application JAR
explanation: Keeping the definition in the repository means it is reviewed, versioned, and branched together with the application code, so changes to the build are traceable.

question: What is a runner (or agent) in a CI system?
options: A developer who monitors the build
A machine or process that executes the jobs of a pipeline
A Git command that uploads commits
A file that stores environment variables
explanation: The CI server schedules jobs, and runners or agents are the workers that actually run the commands. They can be hosted by the provider or self-managed.

question: How does a CI pipeline typically learn that new code was pushed?
options: Developers must email the CI administrator
It only runs on a manual button press
It reads the developer's local disk
The repository sends an event (such as a push or pull request webhook) that triggers the pipeline
explanation: Hosting platforms notify the CI system through webhooks or built-in integration. Pipelines can also be started by schedules or manually, but event triggers are the standard.

question: When does this workflow run?
code:
name: CI
on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: mvn -B verify
options: When a pull request targets the main branch
On every push to any branch
Only when a tag is created
Only when started manually
explanation: The on section lists pull_request with a branches filter for main, so the workflow runs for pull requests whose base branch is main. Pushes and tags are not listed.

question: Why is the -B option commonly used in the command mvn -B verify inside a pipeline?
options: It skips all tests
It runs Maven in the background
It runs Maven in non-interactive batch mode, which suits CI because no one can answer prompts
It enables remote debugging
explanation: Batch mode disables interactive prompts and simplifies the output, which is appropriate for unattended CI runs. It does not change which phases run.

question: A pipeline step compiles this program and runs it with java Check. Assume Java 17. What is the result of the step?
options: The step succeeds because the program printed output
A compile-time error is reported
A NullPointerException is thrown
The program prints tests and exits with a non-zero status, so the step is marked failed
explanation: CI tools judge a step by its exit code. Zero means success, any other value means failure. System.exit(1) ends the JVM with status 1 after the output is printed.

question: What is a pipeline artifact?
options: A bug found by the pipeline
A file produced by a job, such as a JAR or test report, saved so later jobs or people can use it
A secret value stored by the CI system
A Git tag created by the pipeline
explanation: Artifacts are job outputs that are stored after the job finishes. Later stages can download them, and people can inspect them, for example test reports.

question: Why do pipelines usually cache the Maven local repository?
options: To guarantee that all tests pass
To store passwords safely
To avoid downloading the same dependencies in every run and so shorten build time
To permanently archive release builds
explanation: A cache reuses data from earlier runs. Dependency downloads are slow and repeated, so caching them speeds up the pipeline. A cache is an optimization and may be missing, so the build must still work without it.

question: What should a good dependency cache key be based on?
options: A hash of pom.xml (or the lock file), so the cache refreshes when dependencies change
The current time in seconds, so each run gets a new cache
The name of the developer who pushed
A constant string that never changes
explanation: Keying the cache on the dependency file means it is reused while dependencies are unchanged and rebuilt when they change. A constant key may serve stale data, and a time-based key never reuses anything.

question: What is the benefit of running independent jobs in parallel in a pipeline?
options: It guarantees fewer bugs
It removes the need for tests
It lets jobs share the same memory
Independent jobs run at the same time on separate runners, which reduces total pipeline time
explanation: Jobs that do not depend on each other can run concurrently, so total time is closer to the longest job than to the sum of all jobs.

question: How many jobs does this matrix create (assuming no other matrix keys)?
code:
strategy:
  matrix:
    java: [11, 17, 21]
explanation: A matrix creates one job for each value combination. With a single key of three values, there are three jobs, one per Java version.

question: What does the fail-fast principle mean for pipeline design?
options: Stop early when something fails and run cheap, quick checks first so developers get feedback quickly
Run every job even after a failure to hide the error
Only run tests on Fridays
Retry failed jobs forever until they pass
explanation: Failing fast saves resources and gives quick feedback. Cheap checks such as compilation and linting run before slow tests, so obvious problems stop the pipeline sooner.

question: How should a pipeline receive a database password for integration tests?
options: Commit it in application.properties
Hardcode it in the Dockerfile
Store it in the CI secret store and inject it as a masked environment variable
Write it in the README for the team
explanation: Secrets must not be committed to the repository, because history keeps them forever. The CI secret store injects them at runtime and masks them in logs.

question: The program runs on a laptop where the environment variable CI_BUILD_NUMBER is not defined. What is printed? Assume Java 17.
options: build-null
A NullPointerException is thrown
local
build-
explanation: System.getenv returns null for an undefined variable instead of throwing. The null check selects the local branch, so local is printed.

question: What is a flaky test and how should it be handled?
options: A test that sometimes passes and sometimes fails without code changes, which should be diagnosed and fixed or quarantined
A test that always fails, so it should be deleted
A test that runs very slowly, so it should be rerun until it is green
A test written in a different language
explanation: Flaky tests erode trust in the pipeline. Rerunning until green hides the problem. The root cause, often timing, shared state, or external dependencies, should be fixed, or the test quarantined meanwhile.

question: Using the stated rule, which stages are executed (including the failed one)?
code:
stages = [build, test, deploy]
rule: a stage runs only if all previous stages succeeded
build succeeds
test fails
print the stages that were executed, in order
options: build test deploy
build test
build
test deploy
explanation: Build runs and succeeds, test runs and fails. Because a stage requires all earlier stages to succeed, deploy is skipped.

question: How many jobs does this pipeline create?
code:
os = [linux, windows]
java = [11, 17, 21]
jobs = every combination of os and java
remove the combination (windows, 11)
print number of jobs
explanation: Two operating systems times three Java versions gives six combinations. Removing one excluded combination leaves five jobs.

question: Which pipeline stage typically produces the deployable file, such as a JAR, for a Java service?
options: The build or package stage
The notification stage
The code review stage
The branch deletion stage
explanation: The build or package step compiles the code and creates the JAR. Later stages test, publish, or deploy that same output.

question: Which statement about an idempotent pipeline step is correct?
options: It runs only once in the lifetime of the project
It always deletes the workspace afterwards
Running it repeatedly with the same input gives the same result without harmful extra side effects
It can only be written in Groovy
explanation: Idempotent steps are safe to retry or rerun. This matters because pipelines are rerun after failures, and a step like create-the-release would break if it fails on the second run.

question: Complete the step so that the pipeline uses JDK 17.
code:
- uses: actions/setup-java@v4
  with:
    distribution: temurin
    java-version: ____
options: 'JDK17'
'java17.0.x-lts'
explanation: The java-version input takes the version number, here 17. The other values are not valid version strings for this action.

question: This workflow is rejected as invalid. What is the cause?
code:
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
  steps:
    - run: mvn -B test
options: The runs-on key is not allowed in a job
The steps key is at the wrong indentation level and must be nested under the build job
The command must be mvn verify
Job names must be written in uppercase
explanation: In YAML, indentation defines structure. Here steps is a sibling of build instead of belonging to it, so the job has no steps and an unexpected job appears.

question: What does the build once, deploy many principle recommend?
options: Build the artifact once and promote the same artifact through test, staging, and production
Rebuild the code separately for every environment
Build only on the production server
Build once per year
explanation: Promoting the identical artifact ensures that what was tested is what gets deployed. Rebuilding per environment may produce differences.

question: A pipeline contains only a compile step and no tests, and it passes. What does that prove?
options: The code has no bugs
The application is ready for production
Only that the code builds, not that its behavior is correct
That tests are unnecessary
explanation: A green pipeline proves only what its checks verify. Without tests, correctness is not checked at all.

question: When does this schedule trigger run (GitHub Actions, which uses UTC for schedules)?
code:
on:
  schedule:
    - cron: '0 2 * * *'
options: Every 2 minutes
Every day at 02:00 UTC
Every Sunday at 02:00 UTC
Every 2 hours
explanation: The cron fields are minute, hour, day of month, month, and day of week. Minute 0 and hour 2 with wildcards for the rest means daily at 02:00.

question: Why configure a pipeline to cancel older in-progress runs for the same branch when a new commit is pushed?
options: To hide failing tests
To make the older run pass
To delete the branch
To save runner resources and avoid testing outdated code
explanation: If a newer commit supersedes the older one, finishing the old run wastes resources and can confuse results. Concurrency settings can cancel it.

question: A push changes only README.md. What happens with this workflow?
code:
on:
  push:
    paths:
      - 'src/**'
options: The workflow runs because any push triggers it
The workflow runs but skips all steps
The workflow fails with a syntax error
The workflow is not triggered
explanation: The paths filter limits the trigger to pushes that change files under src. A change to only README.md does not match, so no run starts.

question: What is the purpose of a manual approval gate before a production deployment?
options: To make the build faster
To let a responsible person confirm the release, as in continuous delivery
To replace automated tests
To delete old artifacts
explanation: A manual gate pauses the pipeline until someone approves. This keeps a human decision at the release point while everything before it stays automated.

question: Why can printing a transformed secret in the build log still leak it, even though the CI system masks secrets?
options: Masking is disabled when a job succeeds
Secrets are always printed in clear text
Masking matches the exact secret value, so an encoded or modified form may not be hidden
The log is encrypted only for administrators
explanation: Log masking looks for the literal secret text. If a script prints a Base64 version or splits the value, the mask may not match. The safe rule is never to print secrets.

question: In which order do the stages of this Jenkins pipeline run?
options: Build first, then Test, one after the other
Test first, then Build
Both stages run in parallel
Only Build runs
explanation: Stages in a declarative pipeline run sequentially in the order they are written, unless a parallel block is used.

question: How do webhook triggers differ from polling triggers?
options: Polling is always faster than webhooks
Webhooks notify CI immediately when an event happens, while polling checks the repository at intervals
Webhooks need no network connection
Polling works only for tags
explanation: With a webhook the repository pushes the event to CI. With polling the CI system asks repeatedly, which adds delay and load.

question: The CI job runs this program with java AssertDemo, without any -ea option. Assume Java 17. What is the output?
options: Exception in thread main java.lang.AssertionError: fail
A compile-time error
Nothing is printed
done
explanation: Assertions are disabled by default in the JVM, so the assert statement is skipped. Tests that rely on assert silently do nothing unless the JVM runs with -ea.

question: Why should CI run on every pull request before it is merged?
options: To detect integration problems before the change reaches the main branch
To count the number of commits
To rename the branch automatically
To delete the pull request after an hour
explanation: Running the pipeline on a pull request validates the change early, and required checks can then block merging until it is green.

question: The script runs in Bash and mvn -B test fails with a non-zero exit code. What happens?
code:
set -e
mvn -B test
echo deploying
options: It prints deploying anyway
It prints deploying and then exits with status 0
The script stops at the failed command, does not print deploying, and exits with a non-zero status
The script retries mvn automatically
explanation: set -e makes the shell exit as soon as a command fails. Without it, the next line would run even after a failed test run, which could deploy broken code.

question: What does needs: build do in the test job?
code:
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: mvn -B package
  test:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: mvn -B test
options: It runs both jobs at the same time
It makes the test job wait for the build job and run only if the build succeeds
It copies the steps of build into test
It disables the build job
explanation: needs defines a dependency between jobs. Without it, jobs in a workflow run in parallel by default.

question: Why is using a floating tag such as latest for a build image or action risky?
options: Floating tags are not allowed in any pipeline
It makes the build slower by a fixed amount
It always downloads old versions
The content behind the tag can change, so builds may break or differ unexpectedly; pinning a version keeps them reproducible
explanation: A tag like latest moves. The same pipeline file may behave differently next week. Pinning to a specific version improves reproducibility.

question: What is a trade-off of self-hosted runners compared with provider-hosted runners?
options: They cannot run Java builds
They are always cheaper and need no maintenance
You control hardware and installed tools, but you must maintain and secure them
They remove the need for a pipeline file
explanation: Self-hosted runners give flexibility, for example special hardware or network access, but the team is responsible for updates, capacity, and security.

question: Why are repository secrets usually not exposed to workflows triggered by pull requests from forks?
options: Untrusted code in the fork could print or steal them
Forks cannot run pipelines at all
Secrets are deleted after every merge
Secrets only work on Mondays
explanation: A fork pull request can contain changed pipeline or test code written by anyone. Exposing secrets to it would let a malicious contributor exfiltrate them, so platforms withhold them by default.

question: The test fails on attempts 1 and 2, and passes on attempt 3. What does the pseudocode print?
code:
attempts = 0
while attempts < 3:
    attempts = attempts + 1
    if attempts == 3: result = pass else: result = fail
    if result == pass: break
print attempts
explanation: The loop increments attempts to 1 and 2 with failures, then to 3 where the result is pass and the loop breaks. The value printed is 3.

question: Why should pipeline jobs have a timeout?
options: To make tests pass faster
To increase the number of artifacts
To stop hung jobs from occupying runners indefinitely
To rename the job
explanation: A stuck process, for example a test waiting forever on a network call, would block a runner. A timeout ends the job and frees the resource.

question: The step runs on a runner configured with JDK 17 and executes this program. What is printed?
explanation: Runtime.version().feature() returns the feature release number as an int, which is 17 for JDK 17. Printing it confirms which JDK the pipeline really uses.

question: Why does a workflow normally include a checkout step such as actions/checkout?
options: It deletes old branches
The runner starts with an empty workspace, so the repository code must be fetched into it
It uploads artifacts
It starts the database
explanation: A fresh runner does not contain the project. The checkout step clones the commit that triggered the run so later steps can build it.

question: Why do pipelines usually define an artifact retention period?
options: Because artifacts expire only after the code is deployed
To make artifacts executable
To limit storage use by deleting old artifacts after a set time
To rename the artifacts
explanation: Stored artifacts consume space. Retention policies remove them after a number of days, while release builds are published to a long-term repository instead.

question: A pipeline step runs git describe --tags and fails. The workflow uses the default checkout settings. What is a likely cause?
options: Only the latest commit is fetched by default (shallow clone), so history and tags needed by the command may be missing unless full depth is requested
Git cannot run on a runner
Tags are forbidden in pipelines
The build is running on the wrong operating system by definition
explanation: Many CI checkouts fetch only one commit for speed. Commands that need history, such as describe or diffing against main, require a deeper fetch, for example fetch-depth set to 0.

question: Which event starts this workflow?
code:
on:
  push:
    tags:
      - 'v*'
options: Pushing a branch whose name starts with v
Pushing a tag whose name starts with v
Pushing any commit to main
Opening a pull request
explanation: The tags filter limits the push trigger to tags matching the pattern v*, such as v1.2.0. Branch pushes do not match it.

question: The build passes locally on JDK 17 but fails in CI with the error release version 17 not supported. The CI runner has JDK 11. What is the right fix?
code:
<properties>
    <maven.compiler.release>17</maven.compiler.release>
</properties>
options: Skip tests with -DskipTests
Change the release value to 21
Run mvn clean twice
Configure the pipeline to use JDK 17, for example with a setup-java step
explanation: The compiler can only target a release supported by the JDK that runs it. The pipeline must provide the same JDK version the project requires, which also keeps local and CI builds consistent.

question: Which rule should a team remember about a failed build on the main branch?
options: Ignore it until the next release
Fix or revert it quickly so the main branch stays green and usable
Disable the pipeline to avoid noise
Wait for the failing test to pass by itself
explanation: A broken main blocks everyone, because new work starts from it and further failures hide behind the existing one. Quick repair or revert is the standard CI discipline.

question: What is the total pipeline time?
code:
job A takes 4 minutes
job B takes 6 minutes
job C takes 3 minutes
A and B start together and run in parallel
C starts after both A and B finish
ignore queue time
print total pipeline minutes
explanation: A and B run in parallel, so that phase lasts as long as the slower job, 6 minutes. Then C adds 3 minutes, giving 9 minutes.

question: How does a pipeline cache differ from a pipeline artifact?
options: A cache is an optimization for reusing data like dependencies between runs and may be absent, while an artifact is an output of a run that must be kept for later jobs or download
A cache is always bigger than an artifact
They are the same thing under two names
A cache stores secrets while an artifact stores logs
explanation: Builds must work even when the cache is missing. Artifacts are real products of the run, such as a JAR or report, that later stages depend on.

question: Why are deployment environments such as production often given their own protection settings and secrets?
options: Because environments cannot share code
To make staging slower
Because secrets must be written in the pipeline file
To restrict who can deploy, require approval, and keep production credentials away from less trusted jobs
explanation: Environment settings limit which jobs and people can reach production credentials and can add required reviewers. This reduces the risk of accidental or malicious production changes.

question: Complete the GitLab CI job so that the test report is stored after the job, even when the job fails.
code:
test:
  stage: test
  script:
    - mvn -B test
  ____:
    when: always
    reports:
      junit: target/surefire-reports/TEST-*.xml
options: variables
cache
image
artifacts
explanation: The artifacts keyword saves job outputs. The when: always setting keeps them even when the job fails, which is exactly when test reports are most useful.

question: What is the effect of adding [skip ci] to a commit message on many CI systems?
options: The pipeline is skipped for that commit, which can bypass checks and should be used carefully
The commit is rejected by Git
The pipeline runs twice
All tests run in debug mode
explanation: Many CI platforms recognize skip markers and do not start a pipeline. They are handy for documentation-only changes but risky, because they skip the safety net.

question: The CI job compiles this class and runs java -Dapp.env=staging Config. What is printed? Assume Java 17.
options: dev
null
staging
app.env
explanation: -D defines a system property, and getProperty returns its value. The default dev is used only when the property is absent.

question: In Maven's default lifecycle, which command runs unit tests and also the integration tests bound to the Failsafe plugin?
options: mvn test
mvn verify
mvn compile
mvn validate
explanation: Failsafe runs integration tests in the integration-test phase and checks results in verify. The test phase stops before them, so mvn test alone does not run them.

question: What is a blue-green deployment?
options: Two identical environments are kept, and traffic is switched from the old one to the new one, which also allows quick rollback
Releasing to a small percentage of users first
Deploying only at night
Deploying without any tests
explanation: One environment serves users while the other receives the new version. After verification, traffic switches over, and switching back is the rollback.

question: Which deployment strategy releases a new version to a small subset of users first, before wider rollout?
options: Blue-green deployment
Recreate deployment
Big-bang deployment
Canary release
explanation: A canary release exposes the new version to a small share of traffic. If metrics look healthy, the share grows; otherwise it is rolled back with limited impact.

question: When does this deploy job run?
code:
deploy:
  needs: test
  if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' && github.event_name == 'push'
  runs-on: ubuntu-latest
  steps:
    - run: ./deploy.sh
options: For every pull request
Only for a push event on the main branch, after the test job succeeds
For every tag
Never, because the condition is invalid
explanation: Both parts of the condition must be true: the ref is main and the event is a push. Pull request runs therefore skip deployment, and needs adds the dependency on test.

question: A pull request pipeline was green, but the build fails on main right after merging. What is a plausible explanation?
options: Green pipelines are always wrong
Git deleted the tests during the merge
The pull request was tested against an older base, and the combination with newer main changes broke something
The runner forgot the code
explanation: A pull request check tests the branch as it was, not necessarily combined with the latest main. Two individually correct changes can conflict semantically. Merge queues or merged-result pipelines test the combination before merging.

question: Which Maven command compiles the code and runs the unit tests, but stops before creating the JAR file?
options: mvn test
mvn package
mvn install
mvn deploy
explanation: Maven phases run in order: validate, compile, test, package, verify, install, deploy. Running a phase also runs all phases before it, so mvn test stops after the test phase. mvn package would continue and create the JAR.

question: What does mvn clean do?
options: Runs the unit tests
Packages the project as a JAR
Deletes the target directory with previous build output
Uploads artifacts to a remote repository
explanation: clean belongs to a separate clean lifecycle and removes the target directory. It does not compile, test, or package anything. CI often runs clean so that stale files from older builds cannot affect the result.

question: How do mvn package and mvn install differ?
options: package uploads the artifact to a remote server, while install does not
install also copies the artifact into the local Maven repository, while package only creates it under target
They are identical commands
install skips the tests
explanation: Both run through the package phase. install continues to the install phase, which copies the artifact into the local repository (~/.m2) so other local projects can use it. Uploading to a remote repository is the deploy phase.

question: Which command runs the full Gradle build, including the tests, with the project wrapper on Linux or macOS?
options: ./gradlew clean
./gradlew assemble
./gradlew compileJava
./gradlew build
explanation: The build task runs assemble and check, and check includes the tests. assemble only produces the outputs, compileJava only compiles, and clean only deletes output.

question: Why do projects commit the Maven or Gradle wrapper files?
options: To make the tests run faster
Because Java cannot compile without them
To remove the need for dependencies
To pin the build tool version in the repository so every developer and the CI server use the same one
explanation: The wrapper downloads the exact build tool version the project declares. This avoids the problem that works on my machine because of different Maven or Gradle versions.

question: In JUnit 5, which annotation marks a method that runs before every test method?
options: @BeforeAll
@BeforeEach
@AfterEach
@Setup
explanation: @BeforeEach runs before each test method, while @BeforeAll runs once before all tests in the class. Setup is not a JUnit 5 annotation. A common trap is using @BeforeAll when each test needs fresh state.

question: A test runner calls beforeEach before every test, as JUnit does. What is the output? Assume Java 17.
explanation: The counter is reset before each test, so each test starts from 0 and prints 1. Without the reset, shared static state would give 12, which is how tests become order-dependent.

question: How do the Maven Surefire and Failsafe plugins differ?
options: Surefire runs unit tests in the test phase, while Failsafe runs integration tests in integration-test and checks the results in verify
Surefire runs integration tests, while Failsafe runs unit tests
Both run only in the deploy phase
Surefire compiles the code, while Failsafe packages it
explanation: Failsafe separates running integration tests from verifying them, so cleanup in post-integration-test can still happen when tests fail. Surefire handles ordinary unit tests earlier in the lifecycle.

question: Which statement describes the test pyramid?
options: Few unit tests and many end-to-end tests
Many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, and the fewest end-to-end tests
Equal numbers of every kind of test
Only manual tests at the top and no tests below
explanation: Unit tests are fast and cheap, so a suite should contain many of them. End-to-end tests are slow and brittle, so they should be few. An inverted pyramid gives slow, flaky pipelines.

question: What does a code coverage percentage measure?
options: Whether the code is free of bugs
How fast the tests run
The number of developers who reviewed the code
The share of code executed by tests, which does not prove the behavior is correct
explanation: Coverage shows which code ran during tests, not whether the results were checked. High coverage with weak assertions gives false confidence.

question: A small assertion helper is used in a test. What is the result? Assume Java 17.
options: Exception in thread "main" java.lang.AssertionError: expected 5 but was 5
ok
A compile-time error
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NullPointerException
explanation: 5L is boxed to a Long and 5 to an Integer. Long.equals(Integer) is false because the types differ, so the helper throws an AssertionError whose message looks confusing. This is the classic assertEquals type trap.

question: What is a quality gate?
options: A branch setting that hides failed tests
A tool that compiles Java to bytecode
A set of measurable conditions the code must meet before it can be merged or released
A server that stores artifacts
explanation: A quality gate turns quality goals into pass or fail rules, such as coverage on new code or no new critical bugs. If a condition fails, the pipeline blocks the merge or release.

question: What is JaCoCo used for?
options: Injecting dependencies into Spring beans
Recording which lines and branches ran during tests and producing coverage reports
Hosting Git repositories
Parsing JSON files
explanation: JaCoCo is a Java code coverage library. A Java agent records execution data while the tests run, and reports and checks are created from that data.

question: A single test calls apply(100, true). Which statement about coverage is correct?
options: Line and branch coverage are both 100%
Branch coverage is 100% but line coverage is lower
Coverage cannot be measured for ternary expressions
The return line counts as covered, but branch coverage is only 50% because the false path never ran
explanation: Line coverage only asks whether the line ran. The ternary has two branches, and only the true branch executed, so branch coverage is half. A second test with member false is needed.

question: Project line coverage is 75%. What happens when the JaCoCo check goal runs with this rule?
code:
<rule>
    <element>BUNDLE</element>
    <limits>
        <limit>
            <counter>LINE</counter>
            <value>COVEREDRATIO</value>
            <minimum>0.80</minimum>
        </limit>
    </limits>
</rule>
options: The build succeeds with only a warning
The rule is ignored for the BUNDLE element
The build fails because line coverage is below the 80% minimum
Coverage is rounded up to 80%
explanation: The check goal compares the covered ratio of lines for the whole bundle with the minimum of 0.80. At 0.75 the rule is violated, and the goal fails the build by default.

question: What is static code analysis?
options: Examining code without executing it to find bugs, style problems, or vulnerabilities
Running the application under load
Measuring the memory used at runtime
Compiling the code with a different JDK
explanation: Static analysis inspects source or bytecode without running the program. It can find problems early, for example possible null dereferences, but it can also report false positives.

question: Which pairing of tools and purposes is correct?
options: Checkstyle checks style rules in the source, while SpotBugs looks for bug patterns in compiled bytecode
Checkstyle finds bugs in bytecode, while SpotBugs checks naming style
Both measure code coverage
Both run integration tests
explanation: Checkstyle enforces conventions such as naming, formatting, and Javadoc. SpotBugs analyzes bytecode for suspicious patterns like null dereferences. JaCoCo, not these tools, measures coverage.

question: Which statement best summarizes the difference between static analysis and unit testing?
options: Static analysis runs the program with test data, while unit tests read the source text
They find exactly the same problems
Unit tests are only for style problems
Static analysis inspects code without running it, while unit tests execute code and verify behavior
explanation: The two techniques complement each other. Static analysis finds suspicious patterns without execution, and tests prove that specific behavior works when the code runs.

question: What does the pseudocode print?
code:
conditions: coverage_new >= 80, new_bugs == 0, duplication <= 3
values: coverage_new = 85, new_bugs = 1, duplication = 2
the gate passes only if all conditions are true
print PASS or FAIL
options: PASS
PASS with warning
ERROR
FAIL
explanation: Coverage and duplication are acceptable, but new_bugs is 1, so new_bugs == 0 is false. Because all conditions must hold, the gate fails.

question: How many tests are executed in this pseudocode?
code:
tests = [T1, T2, T3, T4]
results = [pass, pass, fail, pass]
run tests in order and stop at the first failure
print the number of tests executed
explanation: T1 and T2 pass, and T3 fails. The run stops at that point, so T4 is never executed, and the failing test itself counts as executed.

question: Which Surefire setting lets the build continue even when unit tests fail, which is usually a bad idea for a quality gate?
options: <skipTests>false</skipTests>
<failIfNoTests>true</failIfNoTests>
<testFailureIgnore>true</testFailureIgnore>
<forkCount>0</forkCount>
explanation: testFailureIgnore makes Maven ignore test failures, so the build does not fail. That defeats the purpose of the gate. The other settings do not hide failing tests.

question: What is the difference between -DskipTests and -Dmaven.test.skip=true?
options: -DskipTests compiles the test classes but does not run them, while -Dmaven.test.skip=true also skips compiling them
-DskipTests deletes the tests, while -Dmaven.test.skip=true only runs them
They are completely identical
-DskipTests skips main code, while the other skips test code only
explanation: With -DskipTests the test sources are still compiled, so compile errors in tests are found. With -Dmaven.test.skip=true test compilation is skipped too, which can hide such errors.

question: What does this command do?
code: ./gradlew test --tests "com.example.OrderServiceTest"
options: Runs all tests in the project
Runs only the tests of the class OrderServiceTest
Deletes the class OrderServiceTest
Runs the tests in parallel on all classes
explanation: The --tests option filters the test task by class, method, or pattern. It is useful for quick local feedback, but CI normally runs the full suite.

question: In mutation testing, what does a surviving mutant indicate?
options: The code has no bugs
The mutation tool failed to start
The test run was faster than expected
The tests did not detect the change, so they may be too weak
explanation: A mutation tool makes small changes to the code and reruns the tests. If all tests still pass, the mutant survived, which shows that the tests do not verify that behavior well.

question: What is the output? Assume Java 17.
options: FAIL
PASS
A compile-time error
explanation: The test calls the buggy method but never checks the result, so it always passes. It would even count as coverage. Tests need assertions to detect wrong behavior.

question: Which rule applies to well-written unit tests?
options: They should be independent and not rely on the order in which they run
Each test should use the data left by the previous test
They should share static mutable state to save time
They should always run in alphabetical order
explanation: Independent tests can run in any order or in parallel and fail for one reason. Shared state and order dependence create flaky results that are hard to diagnose.

question: Why would a unit test replace a payment gateway with a mock?
options: To increase the production traffic
To make the test depend on the real network
To skip the assertions
To isolate the unit under test from slow or external systems and control the responses
explanation: A mock stands in for a dependency so the test is fast, deterministic, and can simulate cases such as a declined payment that are hard to trigger with the real service.

question: Which of these is an integration test?
options: Calling a pure method with mocked inputs
Saving an entity through a repository to a real database container and reading it back
Checking a single if statement
Verifying a simple getter
explanation: Integration tests verify that components work together with real collaborators, such as a database. Tests that use mocks for all collaborators or check one method in isolation are unit tests.

question: What is Testcontainers used for?
options: Compiling Java to native code
Starting real dependencies such as databases in disposable Docker containers during tests
Measuring code coverage
Formatting source code
explanation: Testcontainers is a library that starts containers from test code and removes them afterwards. It gives integration tests realistic dependencies without a shared permanent test server.

question: The requirement says a person aged 18 or older is an adult. Which boundary input exposes the bug in this code?
explanation: The condition should be age >= 18. For 18 the code returns false instead of true. Boundary values are where off-by-one errors show up, while 17 and 19 behave correctly.

question: In a Gradle Java project, which lifecycle task usually runs the tests together with other verification tasks such as Checkstyle?
options: check
clean
jar
classes
explanation: The check task is the verification lifecycle task. It depends on test and on analysis tasks added by plugins. build runs assemble and check.

question: What does applying a quality gate to new code instead of the whole codebase achieve?
options: It deletes all old code
It forces every legacy issue to be fixed before any merge
It stops new problems from being added without requiring the team to fix all legacy issues first
It disables static analysis for the whole project
explanation: Focusing on new or changed code keeps quality from getting worse while the old debt is reduced gradually. This approach is often called clean as you code.

question: In SonarQube terminology, what is a code smell?
options: A runtime crash that has already happened in production
A security hole that can be exploited remotely
A failing unit test
A maintainability issue that does not break behavior now but makes the code harder to understand or change
explanation: Sonar separates bugs (likely wrong behavior), vulnerabilities (security risks), and code smells (maintainability problems), such as overly complex methods or duplicated code.

question: Which kind of tool checks third-party libraries for known vulnerabilities?
options: A code formatter
A software composition analysis tool such as OWASP Dependency-Check
A garbage collector
A unit test runner
explanation: Software composition analysis compares the dependencies of a project with databases of known vulnerabilities (CVEs). Static analysis of your own code does not cover flaws in libraries.

question: A test expects an exception for division by zero. What is printed? Assume Java 17.
options: no exception
A compile-time error
caught
Infinity
explanation: Integer division by zero throws ArithmeticException at runtime, so the catch block runs. Infinity appears only for floating-point division.

question: Which practice improves the reproducibility of release builds?
options: Pinning exact dependency versions instead of ranges or LATEST
Using version ranges so the newest library is always picked
Building on a different JDK every time
Depending on SNAPSHOT versions of libraries
explanation: If versions float, the same commit can produce different results on different days. Pinned versions make builds repeatable and failures easier to trace.

question: What does a Maven version ending in -SNAPSHOT mean?
options: A final release that can never change
A version used only by test classes
A deprecated version that was removed
An in-development version whose artifact can change over time
explanation: A SNAPSHOT is a moving target. The same version string can refer to different builds, so release builds should not depend on it.

question: What does the option in this command do in a multi-module build?
code: mvn --fail-at-end verify
options: It ignores all failures and always returns success
It continues building modules that do not depend on the failed module, and the build still fails at the end
It stops at the first failure
It skips all tests
explanation: --fail-at-end (-fae) delays the failure so independent modules still build and report their results. The final result is still a failed build.

question: What does this command do?
code: mvn -pl service -am package
options: Builds the service module and the modules it depends on
Builds only the service module and ignores its dependencies
Builds every module except service
Packages a module named am
explanation: -pl selects the project to build and -am (also make) adds the modules it depends on. Without -am, the dependencies would have to come from a repository.

question: Which JUnit 5 annotation temporarily skips a test method?
options: @Ignore
@Skip
@Disabled
@Pending
explanation: @Disabled is the JUnit 5 annotation. @Ignore belongs to JUnit 4. Disabled tests should be tracked because they quietly reduce protection.

question: Which JUnit 5 assertion verifies that a piece of code throws a specific exception type?
options: assertTrue
assertNull
assertThrows
assertSame
explanation: assertThrows takes the expected exception class and an executable. It fails if nothing is thrown or the wrong type is thrown.

question: What is the output? Assume Java 17.

explanation: 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004 in binary floating point, so == fails. Comparing within a tolerance succeeds, which is why tests use assertEquals with a delta for doubles.

question: How does a stub differ from a mock?
options: A stub verifies interactions, while a mock only returns data
A stub returns predefined answers, while a mock also verifies that the expected interactions happened
They are the same, and both are always real objects
A stub is used only in production
explanation: Stubs supply canned data. Mocks additionally record calls and let the test check them, for example that a method was called once with certain arguments.

question: Complete the test so that it checks the sum of 2 and 3.
options: Calculator.add(2, 3, 0)
new Calculator.add(2, 3)
Calculator().add(2, 3)
new Calculator().add(2, 3)
explanation: add is an instance method, so an object must be created with new Calculator() before calling add(2, 3). The other forms are invalid syntax or call a method that does not exist.

question: A quality gate fails because of a newly introduced vulnerability. What is the correct response?
options: Fix the vulnerability, or review it and mark it as a false positive if it truly is one
Lower the gate threshold so the build passes
Disable the gate for this branch
Merge anyway and fix it next year
explanation: The gate exists to stop new risk. Weakening it defeats its purpose, while fixing the issue or documenting a verified false positive keeps the gate meaningful.

question: Maven reports that no tests were executed for this class. Why?
options: JUnit 5 does not support the @Test annotation
The class is not public, so Maven refuses to compile it
The class name does not match Surefire's default test naming patterns
Tests must be placed in the main source folder
explanation: By default Surefire picks up names such as Test*, *Test, *Tests, and *TestCase. CalculatorChecks matches none of them, so the class is skipped silently. Package-private test classes are fine in JUnit 5.

question: Which statement correctly compares Maven and Gradle?
options: Maven uses Groovy scripts, while Gradle uses only XML
Both tools require no configuration file
Gradle cannot run tests
Maven describes the build declaratively in an XML pom.xml, while Gradle uses a Groovy or Kotlin DSL and supports incremental builds with a build cache
explanation: Maven follows a fixed lifecycle configured in XML. Gradle is based on a task graph with scripts in Groovy or Kotlin and avoids rerunning tasks whose inputs did not change.

question: What is the output? Assume Java 17.
